title: 13  AI Tools
text:
13.1 What a Language Model Produces
AI tools can explain an error, suggest R code and edit a whole project. They can also produce code that runs and answers the wrong question.
The practical question is whether you can check the result. A task is safer to hand to an AI when an error will be obvious or easy to test. It is riskier when a wrong answer looks plausible.
A large language model is trained to predict and generate text from the context it receives. That training includes natural language and a great deal of code. Additional training makes the model better at following instructions and producing useful answers.
The important word here is generate. The model does not retrieve a correct answer from a database. It generates a response that fits your request and the context available to it. This is why it can explain an R error very well, but also invent a function name that sounds as though it should exist.
The model’s wording does not measure its certainty. A correct function name and an invented one can arrive in the same confident tone. People often use hesitation as a clue that another person is unsure; generated text does not provide that clue reliably. Judge an answer from its code, sources and results rather than from how confident it sounds.

title: 13  AI Tools
section: 13.2 Three Ways to Use AI for Code
text:
13.2 Three Ways to Use AI for Code
Broadly, there are three ways to use AI for help with data analysis.

A chatbot. You are likely familiar with chatting with Claude, ChatGPT or Gemini through a web page or app. Chatbots are useful for asking questions, brainstorming and learning about a new method. You can paste in an error message, attach a screenshot or upload a script and ask what went wrong. The chatbot only knows what you give it in that conversation, along with any files or saved project instructions it can access.
An in-editor assistant. This type of assistant lives inside another program. It can see the open script, workbook or other selected project context. It offers completions while you type and answers questions without as much copying between windows. GitHub Copilot in Positron and Copilot in Excel are examples. The convenience is useful, but it also makes suggestions very easy to accept without reading them.
A coding agent. An agent can inspect several files, edit them, run code, read the resulting errors and try again. You give it a task rather than asking for one line of code. This makes an agent much more useful for work that crosses several scripts or files. It also gives the agent more opportunities to make changes you did not intend. Your job shifts from typing each line to defining the task, setting limits and reviewing what changed.

Up to this point, you have mostly used AI through a chatbot. There is also a course chatbot that has access to this textbook and should have more context about the examples and conventions used here. In this module we will begin using AI inside the software where we do the analysis.

title: 13  AI Tools
text:
13.3 Current AI products
There are a handful of companies that are provide most of the AI tools that are currently being used. While this is a dynamic space, I’ve tried to list the current products that are available below to help you get a sense of what is available to you.

Claude is Anthropic’s general chatbot. It accepts documents, spreadsheets, images and code, and conversations can be organized into projects with shared instructions and files. Claude Code is Anthropic’s coding agent. It works with a folder or repository and can inspect files, edit them and run commands. A subscription is needed to access this coding agent.
ChatGPT is OpenAI’s general chatbot. It can work with uploaded files, run data analysis and use tools such as web search. Codex is OpenAI’s coding agent. It can work with a repository, edit files, run commands and show the changes for review.
Gemini is Google’s general chatbot. It is closely connected to Google products such as Drive, Docs and Sheets, and it can accept code files and repositories as context. Google also provides coding assistants based on Gemini, although we will not use them directly in this course.
Microsoft Copilot is Microsoft’s name for a family of AI assistants. There is a Copilot chatbot. However, perhaps more useful, are the tools that are embedded in Miscrosoft products like Word and Excel. The Excel copilot tool can create formulas, summaries and charts using the workbook that is already open.
GitHub Copilot is a coding assistant that works in editors such as Positron, as well as on GitHub itself. It began mainly as an inline code-completion tool, but it now also includes chat and agent modes that can edit several files and run code. We will use GitHub Copilot in the next chapter. Notee that copilot relies on models from Claude, OpenAI, and others.
Cursor is a code editor built around AI assistance. It looks and behaves much like VS Code, but chat, code completion and coding agents are central parts of the editor. It can use models from several AI companies.
Open-source and open-weight models can be downloaded and run on your own computer or on a server you control. This can provide more control over the model and where the data go, although running a capable model may require substantial computing power. Typically, most individual users prefer to use one of the big AI companies rather than these open source products. However, companies that are heavy users have started using free, open source products for mundane tasks, while giving more complex tasks to frontier models from Claude and OpenAI.

Features, access and product names change quickly, so check the current documentation before deciding which one to use.

title: 13  AI Tools
section: 13.4 Eight principles for data analysis with AI
text:
13.4 Eight principles for data analysis with AI

You are still responsible. AI can perform much of the work, but you remain responsible for the data, methods, results, and conclusions. You should understand the analysis thoroughly and be able to explain and defend it.
Use AI to explore, but verify before relying on it. AI is especially valuable for inexpensive exploration. You may have an interesting idea that would take days to code, but an AI agent can investigate it quickly. The result can help you decide whether the idea is worth pursuing. Other agents can help identify obvious problems, but agreement between agents is not proof. If you decide to pursue the the analysis, you must verify the data, code, methods, and results yourself.
Protect your data. Do not provide confidential, personal, proprietary, or sensitive data to an AI system unless that system has been approved for such data. When possible, use de-identified data, synthetic examples, or a description of the data structure.
Manage the context. AI needs the relevant files, definitions, background, and project conventions to do good work. Too little context encourages guessing, but too much irrelevant context can also reduce performance. Maintain a current README.md, data dictionary, or project instruction file that records the information the AI needs. Update it as the project changes. You can also ask your AI agent to continually maintain this and other files that provide them with context in their next session.
Define the task and the desired output. Be explicit about what you want the AI to produce, what constraints it must follow, which files it may use or change, and how it should determine whether the task is complete.
Make AI show and explain its work. Ask the AI to describe its approach, assumptions, data transformations, exclusions, and analytical choices. Require inspectable code and supporting sources where appropriate. An explanation supports understanding, but it does not replace verification.
Use multiple agents and models strategically. Do not rely entirely on one model or one conversation. Use different agents for different roles: one might develop an analysis, another audit it, and another attempt an independent implementation. Give reviewers specific tasks rather than simply asking whether the first answer is correct.
Document the analysis and your use of AI. Preserve the raw data, code, prompts or instructions that materially affected the analysis, and important analytical decisions. Disclose meaningful AI assistance and ensure that someone else could reproduce the final results without relying on the original AI conversation.

title: 13  AI Tools
text:
13.5 Common Failure Modes

Invented functions and packages
A model may suggest a plausible function such as summarise_by() or read_excel_sheet() even when it does not exist. R stops with an error, so this is usually easy to find. Search the package’s official reference before installing a package or changing the script around an unfamiliar function.
In Excel, an invented or unavailable function produces #NAME?. The same error can mean that a real Microsoft 365 function is unavailable in an older Excel version, so check the function’s Microsoft support page and its version list.


Assumed column names
If the model has not seen the data, it may write code for columns named yield, crop and year. The file may use Yield, Crop_Name and Harvest_Year. Supply glimpse() output or a short description of the columns before asking for code. For Excel, supply the exact header row, two or three made-up example rows, the sheet and range, and whether the range is an Excel Table.


Out-of-date syntax
Packages change. An old function or argument may have been replaced since the model’s training data was collected. For example, gather() still appears in older code, while current tidyr uses pivot_longer(). “Superseded” means an older function still works but is no longer recommended; “deprecated” normally warns; “defunct” errors. Package documentation is the check.


Numbers produced without a reproducible calculation
Do not ask a chatbot to calculate a reported statistic from pasted rows and then trust the number. Ask for code, run it in R and keep the calculation in the script. In Excel, every reported number should come from a visible formula rather than a typed constant; use FORMULATEXT when the calculation needs to be audited.


Assumptions from another place
Answers about agriculture may default to US crops, agencies and geography. Saskatchewan data may use rural municipalities rather than counties, SCIC definitions rather than a US crop-insurance program, and bushels per acre rather than another yield unit.
Figure 13.1 shows the same 2025 canola yield in three units. A conversion error can change the numerical scale without causing an R error.








Figure 13.1: The acreage-weighted mean 2025 canola yield in the teaching variety file, reported in three units.





The failures differ in how easy they are to notice. An invented function stops the script. A wrong unit or incomplete join may not.








Figure 13.2: Common failures arranged by whether R is likely to stop the script.

title: 13  AI Tools
text:
13.6 A Silent Failure
The yield file is synthetic teaching data, and the five round crop prices are illustrative placeholders rather than observed 2025 market prices. The question is the average 2025 revenue per acre for spring wheat, canola, barley and oats, weighted by acres; the resulting dollars demonstrate a join and are not a Saskatchewan revenue estimate.
The following code looks reasonable. It filters the yield data, joins prices by crop, calculates revenue and then uses na.rm = TRUE in the weighted mean.


# Load the two files
suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(tidyverse))

d <- read_csv(
  "practice/data/sask_variety_yields.csv",
  show_col_types = FALSE
)
p <- read_csv(
  "practice/data/crop_prices.csv",
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

# Keep recorded yields for four crops in 2025
d25 <- d |>
  filter(
    Year == 2025,
    Crop %in% c(
      "Wheat - Hard Red Spring",
      "Canola/Rapeseed",
      "Barley",
      "Oats"
    ),
    !is.na(Yield),
    !is.na(Acres),
    Acres > 0
  )

# Add the price and calculate revenue per acre
j <- d25 |>
  left_join(p, by = "Crop") |>
  mutate(Revenue = Yield * Price_per_bu)

weighted.mean(j$Revenue, j$Acres, na.rm = TRUE)

> # Load the two files
> suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(tidyverse))
> 
> d <- read_csv(
+   "practice/data/sask_variety_yields.csv",
+   show_col_types = FALSE
+ )
> p <- read_csv(
+   "practice/data/crop_prices.csv",
+   show_col_types = FALSE
+ )
> 
> # Keep recorded yields for four crops in 2025
> d25 <- d |>
+   filter(
+     Year == 2025,
+     Crop %in% c(
+       "Wheat - Hard Red Spring",
+       "Canola/Rapeseed",
+       "Barley",
+       "Oats"
+     ),
+     !is.na(Yield),
+     !is.na(Acres),
+     Acres > 0
+   )
> 
> # Add the price and calculate revenue per acre
> j <- d25 |>
+   left_join(p, by = "Crop") |>
+   mutate(Revenue = Yield * Price_per_bu)
> 
> weighted.mean(j$Revenue, j$Acres, na.rm = TRUE)
[1] 473.3639



The result, $476.79 per acre, is plausible. The crop names do not all match. The price file uses Canola and Spring wheat; the yield file uses Canola/Rapeseed and Wheat - Hard Red Spring. Barley and oats match, while canola and wheat receive NA for price.
Count the failed matches before calculating anything:


nrow(d25)
nrow(j)

d25 |>
  anti_join(p, by = "Crop") |>
  distinct(Crop)

sum(is.na(j$Price_per_bu))

sum(j$Acres[is.na(j$Price_per_bu)]) / sum(j$Acres)

j |>
  count(Crop, price_missing = is.na(Price_per_bu))

> nrow(d25)
[1] 1579
> nrow(j)
[1] 1579
> 
> d25 |>
+   anti_join(p, by = "Crop") |>
+   distinct(Crop)
# A tibble: 2 × 1
  Crop                   
  <chr>                  
1 Canola/Rapeseed        
2 Wheat - Hard Red Spring
> 
> sum(is.na(j$Price_per_bu))
[1] 1184
> 
> sum(j$Acres[is.na(j$Price_per_bu)]) / sum(j$Acres)
[1] 0.8747742
> 
> j |>
+   count(Crop, price_missing = is.na(Price_per_bu))
# A tibble: 4 × 3
  Crop                    price_missing     n
  <chr>                   <lgl>         <int>
1 Barley                  FALSE           263
2 Canola/Rapeseed         TRUE            771
3 Oats                    FALSE           132
4 Wheat - Hard Red Spring TRUE            413



The join preserves all 1,416 rows, but 1,051 rows—and about 87% of the acres—have no price. na.rm = TRUE removes them from the weighted mean, so the reported value describes barley and oats rather than all four crops. Use na.rm = TRUE only after counting the missing values and explaining their source.








Figure 13.3: Rows in the 2025 yield data according to whether the join found a crop price.





Reconcile the two known names, repeat the join and check again:


# Reconcile crop names with the price table
d25_fixed <- d25 |>
  mutate(Crop = case_match(
    Crop,
    "Canola/Rapeseed" ~ "Canola",
    "Wheat - Hard Red Spring" ~ "Spring wheat",
    .default = Crop
  ))

# Repeat the join and state the expected relationship
j_fixed <- d25_fixed |>
  left_join(
    p,
    by = "Crop",
    relationship = "many-to-one"
  ) |>
  mutate(Revenue = Yield * Price_per_bu)

sum(is.na(j_fixed$Price_per_bu))
stopifnot(!anyNA(j_fixed$Price_per_bu))
weighted.mean(j_fixed$Revenue, j_fixed$Acres)

> # Reconcile crop names with the price table
> d25_fixed <- d25 |>
+   mutate(Crop = case_match(
+     Crop,
+     "Canola/Rapeseed" ~ "Canola",
+     "Wheat - Hard Red Spring" ~ "Spring wheat",
+     .default = Crop
+   ))
> 
> # Repeat the join and state the expected relationship
> j_fixed <- d25_fixed |>
+   left_join(
+     p,
+     by = "Crop",
+     relationship = "many-to-one"
+   ) |>
+   mutate(Revenue = Yield * Price_per_bu)
> 
> sum(is.na(j_fixed$Price_per_bu))
[1] 0
> stopifnot(!anyNA(j_fixed$Price_per_bu))
> weighted.mean(j_fixed$Revenue, j_fixed$Acres)
[1] 567.6195



The corrected result is $571.17 per acre. In Excel, XLOOKUP would expose unmatched names as #N/A; do not let an AI hide them with IFERROR(...,0), and avoid VLOOKUP without an explicit exact-match argument. Count missing results with =SUMPRODUCT(--ISNA(price_range)) before calculating revenue.
Supplying the price table’s exact crop names in the prompt could have prevented this case. The checks that catch it regardless of the prompt are anti_join(), before-and-after row counts, a missing-value count, and the stopifnot() guard.

title: 13  AI Tools
section: 13.7 Tasks That Are Easy to Check
text:
13.7 Tasks That Are Easy to Check
AI assistance is useful when the result can be tested quickly:

Explain an R error message and identify the line it refers to.
Suggest the name of a function, followed by a check of its documentation.
Draft repetitive syntax such as a case_when() block.
Explain an unfamiliar line of code.
Produce a first draft of a plot whose labels, groups and values can be inspected.
Explain an Excel error such as #SPILL!, #VALUE! or #REF!, followed by checking the referenced cells.
Draft a SUMIFS or XLOOKUP, followed by filtering the source table and checking matching rows.

In each case, R or the user provides a separate check.

title: 13  AI Tools
text:
13.8 Tasks Requiring More Judgment
Some tasks require information the model does not have:

Choosing the analysis without a clear question.
Deciding whether the observations represent the population of interest.
Judging whether an agricultural result is plausible in its stated units and location.
Choosing which caveat matters to a producer, client or policy maker.
Supplying references that have not been checked against the original source.

AI can help list possibilities, but the final decision has to be justified from the question, data and subject matter.

title: 13  AI Tools
section: 13.9 Data That Should Not Be Sent
text:
13.9 Data That Should Not Be Sent
Prompts and code sent to a hosted AI service leave the computer. What is stored, for how long, and whether it is used to improve a service depends on the provider, account and organization settings.
The datasets in this course are public or synthetic. A producer’s field records, financial statements, contact information, employee data and material covered by a confidentiality agreement are different. Do not paste someone else’s confidential data into a consumer AI tool. Describe the column names, types and problem without supplying the values, or use a service approved by the organization that owns the data.
An in-editor assistant may use the current file or other project context. Check what context has been selected and close or exclude files that should not be sent (Section 14.3).
Copilot in Excel sends Table content to Microsoft’s service; it is not a local calculation. An organization-managed Microsoft 365 account may operate within that organization’s data protections, while a consumer chatbot account does not inherit them. Follow the data owner’s policy and use headers plus made-up rows when approval is uncertain.

title: 13  AI Tools
text:
13.10 Course Policy
AI tools may be used for module practice and the course project. They may not be used on tests.
Tests check whether you can read the data, choose an analysis and recognize an implausible answer without the tool doing those jobs for you. For submitted work, you must be able to explain every line of code and account for every reported number.
A 2026 working paper reports an observational comparison involving 26,811 Chinese secondary students who self-selected into using generative AI (Strömberg et al. 2026). After adoption, homework scores rose and completion times fell, while exam scores fell.






Figure 13.4: Changes in homework scores, completion time and exam scores after students began using AI, compared with students who had not. Source: Strömberg, Lei and Wu (2026).



The paper argues that students substituted the tool for practice. That is a plausible interpretation, but its subgroup comparison contrasts students who chose to change their work differently; it is not a clean experimental test of the mechanism. The result therefore does not imply that every use of AI reduces learning.
Other courses have their own rules. Check the syllabus for each course before using AI on assessed work.

title: 13  AI Tools
text:
13.11 The Rest of This Module
The next chapter sets up GitHub Copilot as a provider for Positron Assistant and develops a checking routine. The final chapter uses graphing exercises because a visible figure makes many coding errors easier to inspect. This module practises AI assistance mainly in Positron because scripts make the generated work visible; the same checking habits apply to formulas and charts produced by Copilot in Excel.






TipOther resources – AI-assisted coding






3Blue1Brown, But what is a GPT? gives a visual explanation of language-model prediction.
Simon Willison, Not all AI-assisted programming is vibe coding develops the explanation standard used above.








Strömberg, David, Victor Lei, and Yanhui Wu. 2026. The Generative AI Learning Penalty: Evidence from Chinese Secondary Education. CEPR Discussion Paper No. DP21577. Centre for Economic Policy Research. https://cepr.org/publications/dp21577.

title: 14  GitHub Copilot
text:
14.1 Getting Access
The AI coding assistant we will use for this course is GitHub Copilot. This assistant works well within the Positron environment. It can function at all three levels of AI assistance – as a chatbot, an inline editor, and an agent. Most importantly, it is free for students and faculty.
Note that GitHub Copilot and Microsoft 365 Copilot are separate products. GitHub Copilot supplies coding help in Positron and is the product used here. Copilot in Excel requires separate Microsoft licensing; GitHub Education does not unlock it.
A GitHub Pro plan is free for post-secondary students and faculty. This provides you with the equivalent of $15 of monthly credits, which should be more than enough for our class. To apply for the student benefit:
Apply early as verification can take several days.

title: 14  GitHub Copilot
text:
Create a personal account at github.com if you do not have one.
Open your GitHub Education benefits and start a student application.
Add and verify your @usask.ca address if GitHub asks for an academic email.
Supply current proof of enrolment, such as a student card with an enrolment date, a class schedule, a transcript or an enrolment letter.
After verification, return to the benefits page and activate the Copilot benefit. Education approval and Copilot activation are separate steps.

title: 14  GitHub Copilot
text:
14.2 Connecting Copilot to Positron
You can connect to Github Copilot directly through Positron using these steps:

Update Positron before beginning.
Open View > Command Palette, or use Cmd+Shift+P on macOS or Ctrl+Shift+P on Windows.
Run Authentication: Configure Language Model Providers.
Select GitHub Copilot and sign in through the browser window that opens.
Return to Positron and open Posit Assistant chat. Copilot should appear as an available provider.









A. View → Command Palette.







B. The Authentication: Configure Language Model Providers command.






Figure 14.1: Connecting Copilot through the Command Palette.



Copilot’s grey inline completions become available after the same sign-in. If chat or completions do not appear, restart Positron. If the account was connected in an older Positron release, sign out of GitHub from the Accounts menu and sign in again.
The command AI: Create Diagnostic Report lists the active providers and AI settings without exposing the content of your prompts. It is the quickest check when Positron appears connected but produces no suggestions.
These command names were checked in August 2026. If a later Positron release uses different wording, search the Command Palette for “language model” or “AI” and consult the configuration page linked below.

title: 14  GitHub Copilot
text:
14.3 Two Ways to Use It

Inline completions
Inline completions appear as grey text while you type. Press Tab to accept a suggestion, Esc to dismiss it or keep typing to replace it.
In Figure 14.2 the AI is trying to helpfully suggest how to complete my code to read in a file. Unfortunately, it is completing with the wrong file name! This is because the inline completion is trying to guess what I want from just what is in the existing code – since it knows from my comment that I want to load variety data, it makes the, not illogical, guess that the raw data is called data/variety_data.csv.






Figure 14.2: An inline completion guessing the wrong file name. The grey text is the suggestion; the real file is sask_variety_yields.csv.



In Figure 14.3, I want to summarize the columns in the data. More helpfully, once I start typing summa it correctly guesses that I want to run summary(variety_yields).






Figure 14.3: After a few letters, the completion supplies the whole call.



Inline completion is useful for predictable syntax, repeated arguments and the next line of a pattern already present in the script. It is a poor place to ask for an explanation because the result arrives as code rather than a discussion.


Posit Assistant chat
More powerful is the Posit Assistant chat. You can open it from the sidebar, as shown in Figure 14.4.








A. The Posit Assistant icon in the sidebar.







B. The chat pane. Note the reminder at the bottom about which folder the assistant will work in.






Figure 14.4: Opening Posit Assistant.



By default, the assistant can access all the files in your project. Make sure you want to give it this access before proceeding. The assistant also has modes (Figure 14.5) that control how much it does before asking: in Normal mode it asks for approval before most edits, while Auto mode approves more of its own actions.






Figure 14.5: The assistant’s modes. Normal asks for approval before most edits.



Not only can the assistant answer questions about your code, but it can write code for you. In Figure 14.6 I ask it to summarize the yields of each variety. It writes the code, asks permission to run it, and executes it, ensuring that it actually runs.








A. The request.







B. The assistant asks before executing code (in normal mode).






Figure 14.6: Asking the assistant to write a summary.









Figure 14.7: The result: the assistant edited the script, ran it, and reported what it found – including a caveat about varieties with only one observation.



If this isn’t mind blowing enough, it can do much more than that. For example, you can ask it to write a report for you. In the drop down below you can see my very short conversation asking the assistant to generate a report on the most common varieties planted to each crop in 2025. The report it generated is embedded beneath. The report is far from perfect – it has a big table of crop acres that I didn’t want; I just wanted the bar charts it produced. But I can quite easily ask it to remove those tables, alter the graphs, and so on. This is pretty amazing for about a minute of work on my part! The code it wrote is right in the report file for me to validate.






NoteThe full conversation











Figure 14.8: The whole exchange: one request, two answers from me to its clarifying questions, and a rendered report. Notice that it checks the data (the executeCode steps) before writing anything.












NoteThe generated report






The report is also available on its own page.

title: 15  Graphing with AI
text:
Set up the readme file
Graphing is a good place to begin using AI assistance. ggplot2 is a great package, but details such as annotations, direct labels and axis breaks require arguments that are easy to forget and somewhat difficult to implement – for example, getting text in just the right place can take trial and error. An assistant can draft that syntax quickly.
It is also fairly easy to verify the work an AI assistant does on a chart. If you make the raw chart yourself, then you only need to verify that the aesthetics of the graph have been updated correctly, which can be seen visually as opposed to through the code.
This chapter works in R with an assistant in Positron, in three stages: setting up a README the assistant can rely on, iterating on a chart we built ourselves, and then handing the assistant a whole task, from download to report.
Our first thing to do is to establish a readme file that the assistant can refer to. This should establish the structure of the project. We don’t need to be too detailed about the data we are using, because the AI itself can continue to build this readme file.
The common file format is a .md file. You can write this as essentially a plain text file, denoting sections with hashtags. For example, my first README.md is below
That’s it. Save it as README.md at the top of your project folder, beside data/, code/ and output/.
Now we can get the assistant to read our variety data and summarize it for us. With the readme in place, the request can be short, because the standing instructions are already written down:
You could see in your console that the agent is actually running some R code and learning about the data. The output of which it might paste in your chat. For me, it created the following addition to the Readme file:
(The summary was accurate when the assistant wrote it. The dataset has since been extended with risk zones 22 and 23, so the file now has 14,700 rows, and the counts you get will be a little larger.)
Before trusting the summary, check it the same way you would check any other AI output.

title: 15  Graphing with AI
text:
# AREC 261 

I am a student in AREC 261 Agricultural Data Analytics.  In this class, we
will work with several agricultural datasets to learn concepts about data
analysis, data visualization, and data communication.

## Tools

We will be using R for data analysis.

When you write R code ensure that you are using the tidyverse package and
that your code is well-commented so that I can learn.

## Datasets

We will continually re-use datasets.  So when we first encounter a dataset,
update this document with a summary of the data set and what data it
includes.



Read data/sask_variety_yields.csv. Summarize its structure – the columns, what one row represents, the years covered, and anything I should know about missing values – and add that summary to the Datasets section of README.md.


### `data/sask_variety_yields.csv`

Saskatchewan crop variety performance trial data, 13,625 rows and 6 columns. Each row is one crop variety's yield performance in a given risk (soil) zone and year.

- `Risk_Zone`: numeric code (1–21) for the Saskatchewan soil/crop risk zone where the trial was conducted.
- `Crop`: crop type (e.g. Canola/Rapeseed, Wheat - Hard Red Spring, Field Peas, Barley, Lentils, Oats, Flax), 25 distinct values.
- `Variety`: name of the specific crop variety.
- `Year`: trial year, ranging from 2021 to 2025.
- `Acres`: acres of the variety grown/tested for that Crop x Variety x Risk_Zone x Year combination.
- `Yield`: yield (units not confirmed from the file, likely bushels/acre) for that combination.

Each Crop x Variety x Risk_Zone x Year combination is unique (no duplicate keys).

**Missing values:** `Acres` and `Yield` are missing together in the same 4,186 rows (~31% of the data), and never missing individually. Missingness is strongly concentrated in earlier years — about 51% of rows are missing in 2021, dropping steadily to ~0.1% in 2025. This pattern suggests missingness reflects newer varieties without trial history in earlier years, rather than random data loss, but this should be confirmed with the data source before drawing conclusions.







Figure 15.1: The assistant at work: it ran R against the file (left), reported the missingness pattern, and edited the Datasets section of README.md (right).

title: 15  Graphing with AI
text:
15.1 Now for charts
Let’s go back to the line chart we made in the previous session. Below I have the minimal code for producing the last line chart that we created in that chapter.
library(tidyverse)
library(janitor)

# Risk-zone records for all crops, varieties and years
variety_yields <- read_csv(
  "data/sask_variety_yields.csv",
  show_col_types = FALSE
) |>
  clean_names()          # column names to lowercase


# Total acres for each variety and year
barley_by_year <- variety_yields |>
  filter(crop == "Barley") |>
  group_by(variety, year) |>
  summarise(acres = sum(acres, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

barley_by_year

##First get the total acreage of each variety across all risk zones and years
barley_variety_yields <- variety_yields |>
  filter(crop == "Barley") |>
  group_by(variety) |>
  mutate(total_acres = sum(acres, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  ungroup()

## For varieties with less than 150,000 acres across all years, rename them to "Other"
barley_variety_yields <- barley_variety_yields |>
    mutate(variety = if_else(total_acres<150000, "Other", variety))

# Total acres for each variety and year
barley_by_year <- barley_variety_yields |>
  group_by(variety, year) |>
  summarise(acres = sum(acres, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  ungroup()

barley_by_year |>
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = acres, colour = variety)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::comma, limits = c(0, NA)) +
  labs(title = "Acres of barley varieties in Saskatchewan",
       x = "Year", y = "Total acres", colour = NULL) +
  theme_classic(base_size = 13)

## Create plot (as above) and save it as the object variety_line_chart
variety_line_chart <- barley_by_year |>
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = acres, colour = variety)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::comma, limits = c(0, NA)) +
  labs(title = "Acres of barley varieties in Saskatchewan",
       x = "Year", y = "Total acres", colour = NULL) +
  theme_classic(base_size = 13)

## Visualize variety line chart by printing it in the console
variety_line_chart

# Save the finished line chart
ggsave(
  "output/module_4/variety_line_chart.png",
  plot = variety_line_chart,
  width = 6.4,
  height = 4.0,
  dpi = 300
)
In my view the graph is OK. But there are many ways to improve it. My list would be: 1. Includes only the top five varieties and an other category – this means grouping the other varieties into the other category. 2. Include faint gridlines at each 100,000 3. Instead of a legend put variety names directly in the graph 4. The colours are a bit too bright – use a more muted, colour-blind palette
These variations are all quite possible with ggplot. But they are tedious work. The type of tedious work that AI excels at. So let’s ask the assistant to do it for us. The prompt I would use is:

Write a new script that modifies the script in module_4/ch12_02_line_charts.R and produces a final chart that differs from the current output in four ways:

Includes only the top five varieties and an other category – this means grouping the other varieties into the other category.
Include faint gridlines at each 100,000.
Instead of a legend put variety names directly in the graph.
The colours are a bit too bright – use a more muted, colour-blind palette.

Call this script module_5/ch15_updated_line_graph.R

The assistant wrote the script, saved it as code/module_5/ch15_updated_line_graph.R, ran it, and produced the chart below. All four requests are there. It also stretched the x-axis to 2026, a year with no data, to make room for the labels – whether to accept that is your call, not its.






Figure 15.2: The chart produced by the assistant’s script: top five varieties plus Other, direct labels, faint gridlines and a muted palette.



I like this graph more than the first. But there are still some issues. For one, Copilot has a habit of adding information to the graph to demonstrate that it fulfilled your instructions. The subtitle is an example of this. Other things that I don’t like include the colour pallette (still), the all-caps of the variety names, and the fact that 2026 is on the horizontal axis.
My next instruction to the assistant is:

This is good! Now:

Remove the subtitle – always use titles as if you are making the graph for an external audience. Don’t include references to my instructions or past graphs.
Put varieties in proper casing (Synergy AAC)
Move the variety names slightly to the left – cover about half the white space that now exists between the labels and the end of the plots.
Remove 2026 from the horizontal axis
I still don’t love the colours – is there a better standard option for graphs. I particularly don’t like the grey for Synergy.


Giving AI positive feedback (This is good!) is important for two reasons. First, I think we should be nice to AI agents – it enforces habits of politeness that we will draw on in our human relationships and AI may one day come to rule us, hopefully it will be as nice to us in those coming years. Second, it reinforces that we like the job that AI did, which it will learn from.
Its second attempt is here:






Figure 15.3: The second iteration: no subtitle, proper-case labels, a trimmed axis and a new palette.



I’m still not a huge fan of the colour palette. And the direct labels are not quite straight. I’ll ask for two more changes:

Almost perfect! Make sure the labels are all aligned left – right now they are almost exactly in the right place, but they are not all aligned. And use the Okabe-Ito colour palette, avoiding the yellow.

Here is my final result:






Figure 15.4: The third iteration: left-aligned labels and the Okabe-Ito colour-blind-friendly palette.



Importantly, the work of the AI is clearly documented in the code that it produced. Because this is a graph, my standards for going through the code line-by-line are a bit more lax. I can see the data has not changed from my first graph, and the generated code only pertains to the aesthetics of the graph.






NoteThe script the assistant produced: code/module_5/ch15_updated_line_graph.R





library(tidyverse)
library(janitor)

# Risk-zone records for all crops, varieties and years
variety_yields <- read_csv(
  "data/sask_variety_yields.csv",
  show_col_types = FALSE
) |>
  clean_names()          # column names to lowercase

## First get the total acreage of each barley variety across all risk zones and years
barley_variety_yields <- variety_yields |>
  filter(crop == "Barley") |>
  group_by(variety) |>
  mutate(total_acres = sum(acres, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  ungroup()

# Identify the top five varieties by total acres; everyone else becomes "Other"
top_five_varieties <- barley_variety_yields |>
  distinct(variety, total_acres) |>
  slice_max(total_acres, n = 5) |>
  pull(variety)

barley_variety_yields <- barley_variety_yields |>
  mutate(variety = if_else(variety %in% top_five_varieties, variety, "Other"))

# Recase variety names (e.g. "SYNERGY AAC" -> "Synergy AAC"), keeping short
# all-caps breeding-program codes (AAC, CDC, AC) in upper case
recase_variety <- function(x) {
  words <- str_split(x, " ")
  map_chr(words, function(w) {
    w |>
      str_to_title() |>
      (\(w2) if_else(str_length(w) <= 3 & w == str_to_upper(w), str_to_upper(w), w2))() |>
      paste(collapse = " ")
  })
}

barley_variety_yields <- barley_variety_yields |>
  mutate(variety = recase_variety(variety))

# Total acres for each variety (including "Other") and year
barley_by_year <- barley_variety_yields |>
  group_by(variety, year) |>
  summarise(acres = sum(acres, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

# Labels are placed at each line's final year, to replace the legend
label_data <- barley_by_year |>
  filter(year == max(year))

## Create the output folder for this module if needed
dir.create("output/module_5", recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)

variety_line_chart <- barley_by_year |>
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = acres, colour = variety)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  # geom_text (not geom_text_repel) with a fixed x guarantees every
  # label's left edge lines up, since ggrepel can override hjust
  geom_text(
    data = label_data,
    aes(label = variety, x = 2025.15),
    hjust = 0,
    size = 3.5,
    fontface = "bold",
    show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  # Okabe-Ito colour-blind-friendly palette, replacing yellow (#F0E442) and
  # orange (#E69F00) since orange reads as yellow at this size
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(
    "#000000", "#56B4E9", "#009E73", "#0072B2", "#D55E00", "#CC79A7"
  )) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    labels = scales::comma,
    limits = c(0, NA),
    breaks = scales::breaks_width(100000)
  ) +
  # Give labels room to the right of the last data point without cutting them off
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = unique(barley_by_year$year),
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0.02, 0.28))
  ) +
  coord_cartesian(clip = "off") +
  labs(
    title = "Acres of barley varieties grown in Saskatchewan, 2021-2025",
    x = "Year", y = "Total acres"
  ) +
  theme_classic(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "none",
    panel.grid.major.y = element_line(colour = "grey85", linewidth = 0.3),
    plot.margin = margin(t = 5.5, r = 40, b = 5.5, l = 5.5)
  )

## Visualize variety line chart by printing it in the console
variety_line_chart

# Save the finished line chart
ggsave(
  "output/module_5/five_variety_line_chart.png",
  plot = variety_line_chart,
  width = 7.2,
  height = 4.0,
  dpi = 300
)

title: 15  Graphing with AI
text:
15.2 Building a graph from scratch
In the previous example, I asked an AI agent to perfect a graph I had already built. But we can ask AI to do much more – download data, analyze the data, output results, and build reports.
In this example, I will ask the AI to download data on nitrogen fertilizer prices from Statistics Canada from 2018 to present. It should create a graph and on the graph include the text that points to the date of the Russian invasion of Ukraine. It should then write a quick report saying where it obtained the data, what the data is, and what the graph shows.

Download the nitrogen fertilizer price index from Statistics Canada (Table 18-10-0258-01) using the cansim package. Analyze the data in R. Create a graph showing how prices have changed over time and annotate the date of the Russian invasion of Ukraine. Write a short report describing the data source, what the data measure, and the main pattern shown in the graph. The audience for the report is just myself, so that I can verify what you have done. But I will later embed the chart in a report. Save everything needed to reproduce the analysis in this project.

The agent downloaded the table, saved a local copy of the extracted series into data/, and produced the chart, a script and a report.






Figure 15.5: The chart the agent produced from a single instruction.



Two things are worth checking against my instructions. I asked for 2018 to present; the agent plotted the whole series back to 2002. The longer window arguably makes a better chart, but the departure from the instruction is the kind of thing you only find by looking. And in the report below, the agent itself flags that fertilizer prices were rising well before the invasion, so the annotation marks a date, not a cause – exactly the caution the limitations guidance in Section 36.2 asks for in your own writing.






NoteThe script: code/module_5/ch16_nitrogen_fertilizer_price.R





# AREC 261 - Nitrogen fertilizer price index
#
# Downloads StatCan Table 18-10-0258-01 (Farm input price index) via the
# cansim package, extracts the "Nitrogen fertilizers" series for Canada,
# and plots how the index has changed over time, annotating the date of
# Russia's invasion of Ukraine (2022-02-24).
#
# A local copy of the extracted series is saved to data/ so the analysis
# can be re-run without re-downloading from StatCan.

library(tidyverse)
library(cansim)

## ---- Download data ---------------------------------------------------

# get_cansim() caches the table locally after the first download, so
# re-running this script will not repeatedly hit the StatCan API
raw_data <- get_cansim("18-10-0258-01")

# Farm Input Price Index, "Nitrogen fertilizers" component, Canada-level
nitrogen_prices <- raw_data |>
  filter(GEO == "Canada", `Price index` == "Nitrogen fertilizers") |>
  select(date = Date, price_index = VALUE, uom = UOM) |>
  arrange(date)

# Save a local copy so the rest of this script (and future sessions) can
# reproduce the analysis without re-downloading from StatCan
write_csv(nitrogen_prices, "data/nitrogen_fertilizer_price_index.csv")

## ---- Plot --------------------------------------------------------------

invasion_date <- as.Date("2022-02-24")

dir.create("output/module_5", recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)

nitrogen_price_chart <- nitrogen_prices |>
  ggplot(aes(x = date, y = price_index)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9, colour = "#0072B2") +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = invasion_date,
    linetype = "dashed",
    colour = "grey30"
  ) +
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = invasion_date + 120,
    y = max(nitrogen_prices$price_index, na.rm = TRUE),
    label = "Russian invasion\nof Ukraine\n(Feb 2022)",
    hjust = 0,
    vjust = 1,
    size = 3.3,
    colour = "grey30"
  ) +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "2 years", date_labels = "%Y") +
  labs(
    title = "Nitrogen fertilizer price index, Canada",
    subtitle = "Farm Input Price Index, quarterly, 2012 = 100",
    x = "Date",
    y = "Price index (2012 = 100)",
    caption = "Source: Statistics Canada, Table 18-10-0258-01"
  ) +
  theme_classic(base_size = 13) +
  theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_line(colour = "grey90", linewidth = 0.3))

nitrogen_price_chart

ggsave(
  "output/module_5/nitrogen_fertilizer_price_index.png",
  plot = nitrogen_price_chart,
  width = 7.5,
  height = 4.5,
  dpi = 300
)









NoteThe report: output/module_5/nitrogen_fertilizer_price_report.md





# Nitrogen fertilizer price index — verification notes

## Data source

Statistics Canada, Table 18-10-0258-01, "Farm input price index" (formerly
CANSIM 002-0022), downloaded programmatically with the `cansim` R package
(`get_cansim("18-10-0258-01")`). Reproduced with
[code/module_5/ch16_nitrogen_fertilizer_price.R](../../code/module_5/ch16_nitrogen_fertilizer_price.R).
A local snapshot of the extracted series is saved at
[data/nitrogen_fertilizer_price_index.csv](../../data/nitrogen_fertilizer_price_index.csv)
so the analysis does not depend on re-downloading from StatCan.

## What the data measure

The Farm Input Price Index (FIPI) tracks prices paid by Canadian farm
operators for inputs used in agricultural production. This series is
narrowed to:

- **Geography**: Canada (national level; the table also has provincial
  breakdowns)
- **Component**: "Nitrogen fertilizers" (a sub-category of "Fertilizer",
  itself under "Crop production" inputs)
- **Frequency**: quarterly
- **Units**: index, 2012 = 100 (i.e., prices are expressed relative to
  their average level in 2012, not in dollar terms)

The extracted series runs from 2002 Q1 to 2026 Q1 (97 observations).

## Main pattern in the graph

Nitrogen fertilizer prices show two large spikes over the sample period:
one around 2008–09 (index peaking near 126, coinciding with the global
commodity/food price spike of that period) and a much larger one in
2021–22 (index peaking near 172 in early 2022). The 2021–22 rise begins
before the Russian invasion of Ukraine (Feb 24, 2022) — prices were
already climbing sharply through 2021, likely reflecting natural gas
price increases (a key nitrogen fertilizer input) and post-pandemic
supply chain disruption. The index continues rising for a few months
after the invasion before falling back, and by 2023–2024 settles in the
100–115 range, still elevated relative to the pre-2021 range (roughly
75–95). Prices have risen again through 2025 into 2026 (index ~133 as of
2026 Q1).

**Caveat**: the invasion is annotated as a reference point requested for
the chart, but the graph alone cannot establish that the invasion caused
the price spike — the run-up predates the invasion, and other factors
(natural gas prices, general inflation, supply chain conditions) were
also in play concurrently. Treat the annotation as marking a
contextually relevant date, not as evidence of a causal break.

title: 15  Graphing with AI
text:
15.3 Prompting AI
AI output is sensitive to the way you prompt the program. Although AI is becoming better at autonomous work, it still benefits from clear instructions. Here are some tips:

Start with the outcome, not the procedure. Be specific about the deliverables and what it means for the task to be completed.
Ask the agent to verify its own work. Even better, ask the agent to spawn other agents to verify its work. These new agents will not have the context of the working agent, so they are better able to assess the work on its own merits.
Give it the context it needs. Explain what the work is for, what files/data already exist, who the audience is, and any relevant background.
Balance giving constraints with allowing for flexibility. For data analysis, we would definitely want the agent to write R code, as opposed to Python code (assuming we aren’t familiar with the Python language). However, we may not want to specify the exact R functions to use, as the AI may be able to introduce us to new approaches.
Review the agent’s work, not just its final answer. An agent can produce a beautiful graph from the wrong series. Check its source, data selection, code, assumptions, and intermediate decisions. Greater autonomy makes oversight more important, not less.







TipOther resources – ggplot2






ggplot2: Elegant Graphics for Data Analysis, ggplot2-book.org – an explanation of the grammar and its components.
R Graph Gallery, r-graph-gallery.com – examples organized by the kind of chart being built.
ggplot2 reference, ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference – function arguments and current syntax.

title: 16  AI Tools in Excel
text:
16.1 The Three Assistants
The last two chapters used AI from inside Positron, writing R. The same help now exists inside Excel. All three of the major AI companies ship a version of their assistant that sits in a panel beside your spreadsheet, reads the workbook you have open, and – increasingly – edits it for you.
This chapter is short, because the skills are the ones you already have. The prompting habits from Section 13.4 and the checking habits from Section 13.5 carry over directly; only the buttons are new. The landscape also changes monthly, so treat the product details here as a snapshot from mid-2026.
All three do the same family of things. They read the sheets you have open, so you can ask questions about your own data (“which varieties lost acreage between 2021 and 2025?”). They explain what is already there: what a formula does, where a cell’s value comes from, why a lookup returns #N/A. And they write into the workbook: a formula column, a summary table, a chart, a PivotTable.
The differences that matter to a student are access and reach. Copilot is the most deeply integrated but needs a licence your personal Microsoft account probably does not have. ChatGPT’s add-in is the one everyone can try, because it works on a free account. Claude’s requires a paid plan. Check what your university account currently includes before assuming any of them is available on the lab machines.

title: 16  AI Tools in Excel
text:
16.2 What “Agentic” Means in a Spreadsheet
The first generation of these tools was conversational: you asked, it suggested a formula, you pasted the formula in. The current generation is agentic: you describe an outcome, and the assistant plans the steps, executes them in the workbook, inspects its own results, and revises until it is satisfied. Microsoft calls this Agent Mode; Claude and ChatGPT’s add-ins work the same way without the branding.
Concretely, an agent given the barley workbook from Chapter 11 and the instruction “make a bar chart of the varieties with over 10,000 acres, sorted, with labelled axes” will filter, sort, build the chart and format it – the whole sequence Module 4 taught, done in one instruction. Given the messy grain-delivery file from Chapter 8, “clean this up: fix the crop names, flag the impossible weights, and give me a summary by crop” produces a multi-step cleaning pass. The agent is doing real work, in your file, across many cells, without asking about each step.
An assistant that suggests a formula cannot damage anything you did not paste. An agent that edits can overwrite formulas with values, delete a helper column it decides is clutter, or fill a column using a rule you would not have chosen – and a workbook does not keep a record the way a script does. Every result the agent produces was produced by code you never saw.

title: 16  AI Tools in Excel
text:
16.3 Verifying Agentic Work
The checking discipline is the same as Section 13.5, with two Excel-specific habits added:

Work on a copy. Before letting an agent loose on a workbook, duplicate the file, or at minimum the sheet. The raw-data-stays-raw rule (Section 7.6) exists precisely for this moment.
Read the change summary. All three assistants report what they did – cells changed, columns added, steps taken. Read it the way you would read a co-worker’s description of what they did to your file, then spot-check: row counts before and after, one or two values recomputed by hand, totals against the source.
Ask for formulas, not values. An agent pasting the result of a calculation leaves you a dead number; the same calculation as a formula leaves something you can inspect and rerun. If the summary says values were pasted, ask it to redo the step with formulas.
Make it explain. “Walk me through what you did to column D” is a legitimate follow-up, and the explanation is checkable against the cells.

title: 16  AI Tools in Excel
text:
16.4 In This Course
The course policy (Section 13.10) applies unchanged: you may use these tools for practice and for the project, you remain responsible for every number you submit, and the tests are done without them. For the Excel tests in particular, the skills the tests examine – building the chart, writing the lookup, constructing the PivotTable – are exactly the ones the agent would otherwise do for you, which is why they are tested without it.
An agent speeds up work you already know how to check. If you cannot check the work, the speed is not helping you.

title: 17  Thinking Spatially
text:
17.1 Coordinates and reference systems
Almost everything in agriculture happens somewhere: a yield belongs to a field, a rainfall reading to a gauge, an insurance premium to a risk zone. Spatial data is data that keeps the where attached to the numbers, so that location itself can be part of the analysis.
Spatial data comes in two shapes.
Vector data describes things with boundaries or positions: points (a weather station, an elevator), lines (a road, a river), and polygons (a field, a rural municipality, a risk zone). A vector dataset is a table like any other, except that each row carries a geometry column describing its shape. The RM yields we have used all term are one join away from being spatial: Saskatchewan publishes the RM boundaries as polygons, and the RM number links a row of yields to a shape on the map.
Here is that idea in practice. Reading the RM boundaries with the sf package gives a data frame with one extra column:
Each row is an RM; the geometry column holds its polygon. Drawing the table draws the map:
Raster data divides the land into a grid of equal cells and stores one value per cell, like a photograph where every pixel is a measurement. Satellite imagery is raster data, and so is anything derived from it: a 30-metre grid where each cell holds an estimated crop type, a soil-moisture surface, an elevation model.
Here is a small piece of one: a 50-by-50 window of the 2023 Annual Crop Inventory, covering about two square kilometres of central Saskatchewan. Each cell is 30 metres on a side and holds a single value, the crop class:
Zoom in on either figure and the difference between the two shapes is plain: the vector map is exact boundaries, the raster is a grid pretending to be boundaries. Both are tables underneath, which is why the rest of the module can treat them with tools you already have.
A location is usually written as a longitude and a latitude. The two conventions disagree on the order: maps, GPS units and Google write latitude first, while R and most spatial file formats want longitude first, because longitude is the x coordinate and latitude is the y. Figure 17.3 shows the same two numbers entered in both orders.
# A world outline to plot against
world <- map_data("world")

ggplot() +
  # Country outlines in light grey
  geom_polygon(data = world, aes(long, lat, group = group), fill = "grey90") +
  # The field, longitude first
  annotate("point", x = -106.55, y = 52.19, colour = "#4A7C59", size = 3) +
  # The same numbers, latitude first
  annotate("point", x = 52.19, y = -106.55, colour = "firebrick", size = 3) +
  coord_fixed() +
  theme_void()







Figure 17.3: The coordinates of a field near Saskatoon, entered longitude-first (green) and latitude-first (red). The red point is in the Southern Ocean.
Degrees are also not distances. A degree of latitude is about 111 km everywhere, but a degree of longitude shrinks toward the pole – at Saskatchewan’s latitude it is about 68 km. Subtracting two longitudes therefore does not give a distance, an area computed in degrees means nothing, and a map drawn as if degrees were equal in both directions comes out the wrong shape. Figure 17.4 draws the RM centres that way, and the province is stretched wide. geom_sf() drew Figure 17.1 correctly because it knew the coordinates were degrees.
# One point per RM: the centre of its polygon
rm_centres <- rms |>
  st_centroid() |>       # centre point of each polygon
  st_coordinates() |>    # the longitude and latitude of each centre
  as_tibble()

# Degrees plotted as if equal in both directions
ggplot(rm_centres, aes(X, Y)) +
  geom_point(size = 0.4, colour = "grey40") +
  coord_fixed() +
  theme_void()







Figure 17.4: The centre of each RM, plotted as if a degree of longitude equalled a degree of latitude. Compare the shape with Figure 17.1.
A coordinate reference system (CRS) is the statement of what a file’s coordinates mean, and there are two kinds. A geographic CRS records positions in degrees on the globe; the one GPS uses is called WGS 84, or EPSG:4326. A projected CRS flattens a region onto a plane and records positions in metres; most Saskatchewan agency data uses UTM Zone 13. The EPSG number is how software identifies a CRS, and those two – 4326 for degrees, UTM Zone 13 for metres – cover nearly everything in this module.
Every spatial file carries its CRS. Check it rather than guessing: Saskatchewan is wide enough that its western edge falls in UTM Zone 12, so even the usual choice for the province is sometimes wrong. The working rule is to put everything in one CRS before measuring distance or area or combining two layers, and to use a projected CRS when measuring. The functions that check and convert a CRS, st_crs() and st_transform(), are in Chapter 18.
Canadian files sometimes say NAD 83 rather than WGS 84. The two differ by less than a metre here, which is less than a combine header, and this course ignores the difference.

title: 17  Thinking Spatially
text:
17.2 Resolution, scale and extent
Resolution is the size of the smallest thing the data can tell apart. For a raster it is the cell: the Annual Crop Inventory’s cells are 30 metres, so a quarter section is about 27 cells across, and anything smaller than a cell – a slough’s edge, a yard site – is rounded into whichever class dominates the cell. Vector data has a resolution too, in how finely its boundaries are drawn; the RM file this chapter uses has been simplified to within a few hundred metres, which is fine for a provincial map and too coarse for measuring a boundary line. Data also has a resolution in time: a yield monitor logs a point every second, the crop inventory gives one value per year.
Extent is how much ground the data covers: one field for a machinery file, the province for the RM yields, all of Canada for the crop inventory.
The two pull against each other. Fine cells over a large extent make enormous files, so most datasets choose one or the other, and a table’s place on that trade-off tells you what questions it can answer.



Dataset
Resolution
Extent




Yield monitor
a point every second, a few metres apart
one field


Annual Crop Inventory
30-metre cells, once a year
Canada


RM crop yields
one value per RM per year
Saskatchewan


StatCan field crops
one value per province per year
Canada



Matching the data to the question is mostly a matter of direction. Fine data can always be aggregated up to answer a coarse question – yield-monitor points average up to a field mean, ACI cells count up to an RM’s canola area. Going the other way is not possible: an RM yield says nothing about which quarters in the RM did well, and a provincial average hides the differences between RMs.
Figure 17.5 shows what aggregation costs. It is the land from Figure 17.2 again, coarsened so that every 10-by-10 block of cells becomes one 300-metre cell holding the block’s most common class.

# Coarsen the window: each 10-by-10 block of cells becomes one 300 m cell
coarse <- field_classed |>
  mutate(block_x = ceiling(x / 10),
         block_y = ceiling(y / 10)) |>       # assign each cell to a block
  count(block_x, block_y, crop, colour) |>   # cells of each class per block
  arrange(desc(n)) |>                        # most common class first
  distinct(block_x, block_y, .keep_all = TRUE)  # keep it, one per block

# Draw the coarsened cells
ggplot(coarse, aes(block_x, block_y, fill = crop)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white", linewidth = 0.3) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = palette) +
  coord_fixed() +
  theme_void() +
  labs(fill = NULL)







Figure 17.5: The land from Figure 17.2 in 300-metre cells. The large fields survive the coarsening; the wetland, the road allowance and the smaller bluffs are gone.

title: 17  Thinking Spatially
section: 17.3 Where agricultural spatial data comes from
text:
17.3 Where agricultural spatial data comes from

AAFC Annual Crop Inventory. A raster classification of every 30-metre cell of Canadian farmland, produced from satellite imagery every year since 2009: this cell was canola, that one spring wheat, that one was too wet to seed. Accuracy for the major crops is roughly 85 to 90 percent.
Saskatchewan RM boundaries. The polygons for every rural municipality, which is what you need to put the RM yield data on a map.
Canadian Drought Monitor. Monthly drought-condition polygons for the whole country.
Soils. The Saskatchewan Soil Information System maps soil classes and properties across the province.

title: 17  Thinking Spatially
text:
17.4 The Annual Crop Inventory
The Annual Crop Inventory is the dataset this module works with. It answers a question no survey can: not “how much canola did this RM grow” but “what grew in this exact field, each year, going back to 2009.”






TipWhat grew on your land?



This page puts the Annual Crop Inventory on a map. Find a field you know – a home quarter, a field you drive past – and click it to see the classified crop for every year. Field edges and small features misclassify more often than field centres, which is worth remembering whenever you use classified data.


The viewer works by sending a small request to an AAFC server every time you click, and the server answers with the pixel value at that point. That is an API doing its job. In Chapter 23 you make the same kind of request yourself, from R, through Google Earth Engine – and get back data you can tidy, join and plot with the tools you already have.

title: 18  Working with Spatial Data in R
text:
18.1 Reading vector data
Chapter 17 treated spatial data as something to look at. This chapter makes it something to work with. The sf package handles vector data and the terra package handles rasters, and both give you objects that the Module 2 verbs mostly work on unchanged.
The two working files are the RM boundaries from Chapter 17 and a slice of the 2023 Annual Crop Inventory covering two RMs, aci_rm_slice_2023.tif.
st_read() reads most vector formats – GeoJSON, GeoPackage, and shapefiles, which arrive as a folder of files that travel together.
# Load the package for vector spatial data
library(sf)

# Read the RM boundaries
rms <- st_read("data/sask_rms.geojson")

> # Load the package for vector spatial data
> library(sf)
> 
> # Read the RM boundaries
> rms <- st_read("data/sask_rms.geojson")

  using driver `GeoJSON'

Dimension:     XY
Bounding box:  xmin: -110.0057 ymin: 48.99886 xmax: -101.362 ymax: 54.65333

The banner is worth reading before the data: 296 features, geometry type MULTIPOLYGON, a bounding box, and the CRS, WGS 84. Those are the questions Chapter 17 taught, answered before you look at a single row.
# The first rows: a data frame with a geometry column
head(rms, 3)

> # The first rows: a data frame with a geometry column
> head(rms, 3)

Everything from Module 2 applies. filter() keeps rows, select() keeps columns, and the geometry column follows along.

title: 18  Working with Spatial Data in R
text:
18.2 Points from coordinates
A table with longitude and latitude columns becomes spatial with st_as_sf(). The coords argument names the two columns, longitude first, and crs = 4326 states what the numbers mean.


# Four cities as a plain table
cities <- tibble(
  city = c("Saskatoon", "Regina", "Swift Current", "Yorkton"),
  lon  = c(-106.67, -104.61, -107.79, -102.46),
  lat  = c(52.13, 50.45, 50.28, 51.21)
)

# Turn the coordinate columns into point geometry
cities_sf <- st_as_sf(cities, coords = c("lon", "lat"), crs = 4326)

# Print the spatial version
cities_sf

> # Four cities as a plain table
> cities <- tibble(
+   city = c("Saskatoon", "Regina", "Swift Current", "Yorkton"),
+   lon  = c(-106.67, -104.61, -107.79, -102.46),
+   lat  = c(52.13, 50.45, 50.28, 51.21)
+ )
> 
> # Turn the coordinate columns into point geometry
> cities_sf <- st_as_sf(cities, coords = c("lon", "lat"), crs = 4326)
> 
> # Print the spatial version
> cities_sf
Simple feature collection with 4 features and 1 field
Geometry type: POINT
Dimension:     XY
Bounding box:  xmin: -107.79 ymin: 50.28 xmax: -102.46 ymax: 52.13
Geodetic CRS:  WGS 84
# A tibble: 4 × 2

* <chr>             <POINT [°]>
1 Saskatoon     (-106.67 52.13)
2 Regina        (-104.61 50.45)
3 Swift Current (-107.79 50.28)
4 Yorkton       (-102.46 51.21)



Both objects are now layers that can share a map:

# The polygons, then the points on top
ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = rms, fill = "grey97", colour = "grey60", linewidth = 0.1) +
  geom_sf(data = cities_sf, colour = "#4A7C59", size = 2) +
  theme_void()







Figure 18.1: Two vector layers on one map: the RM polygons and four cities as points.

title: 18  Working with Spatial Data in R
text:
18.3 Transforming coordinate systems
st_crs() reports what a layer’s coordinates mean, and st_transform() converts them. Transforming the RMs to UTM Zone 13 turns degrees into metres:


# The CRS the file arrived in
st_crs(rms)$Name

# Convert from degrees to UTM Zone 13 metres
rms_utm <- st_transform(rms, 32613)

# The bounding box before and after
st_bbox(rms)
st_bbox(rms_utm)

> # The CRS the file arrived in
> st_crs(rms)$Name
[1] "WGS 84"
> 
> # Convert from degrees to UTM Zone 13 metres
> rms_utm <- st_transform(rms, 32613)
> 
> # The bounding box before and after
> st_bbox(rms)
      xmin       ymin       xmax       ymax 
-110.00574   48.99886 -101.36201   54.65333 
> st_bbox(rms_utm)
     xmin      ymin      xmax      ymax 
 133976.7 5427372.1  766069.5 6067730.1 



Same province, different numbers: the first box is in degrees, the second in metres. Measurement is the reason to care. With the coordinates in metres, st_area() gives a real area – here, the RM of Corman Park in square kilometres:


# Area of RM 344, Corman Park, in square kilometres
rms_utm |>
  filter(RMNO == "344") |>
  st_area() |>
  as.numeric() / 1e6      # drop the m^2 label, then scale

> # Area of RM 344, Corman Park, in square kilometres
> rms_utm |>
+   filter(RMNO == "344") |>
+   st_area() |>
+   as.numeric() / 1e6      # drop the m^2 label, then scale
[1] 2281.731

title: 18  Working with Spatial Data in R
text:
18.4 Attaching a table to boundaries
The RM boundaries carry no yields, and the RM yield table carries no shapes. The RM number links them. Read the yield file and keep the 2023 canola column:


# Read the wide RM yield file
rm_yields <- read_csv("data/rm_yields_1990plus.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

# One row per RM: 2023 canola
canola_2023 <- rm_yields |>
  filter(Year == 2023) |>
  select(RM, Canola)

# Join the yields onto the boundaries
rm_canola <- left_join(rms, canola_2023, by = c("RMNO" = "RM"))

> # Read the wide RM yield file
> rm_yields <- read_csv("data/rm_yields_1990plus.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
> 
> # One row per RM: 2023 canola
> canola_2023 <- rm_yields |>
+   filter(Year == 2023) |>
+   select(RM, Canola)
> 
> # Join the yields onto the boundaries
> rm_canola <- left_join(rms, canola_2023, by = c("RMNO" = "RM"))
Error: Can't join `x$RMNO` with `y$RM` due to incompatible types.
ℹ `x$RMNO` is a <character>.
ℹ `y$RM` is a <double>.



The join refuses to run: RMNO came out of the boundary file as text and RM is a number. The fix is to make the types agree before joining, and then to check what the join produced:


# Make the key numeric, then join
rm_canola <- rms |>
  mutate(RMNO = as.numeric(RMNO)) |>
  left_join(canola_2023, by = c("RMNO" = "RM"))

# Same 296 rows as the boundaries
nrow(rm_canola)

# RMs with no reported canola in 2023
sum(is.na(rm_canola$Canola))

> # Make the key numeric, then join
> rm_canola <- rms |>
+   mutate(RMNO = as.numeric(RMNO)) |>
+   left_join(canola_2023, by = c("RMNO" = "RM"))
> 
> # Same 296 rows as the boundaries
> nrow(rm_canola)
[1] 296
> 
> # RMs with no reported canola in 2023
> sum(is.na(rm_canola$Canola))
[1] 7



A left join keeps every boundary, so the row count matching rms is the first check, and the count of missing yields is the second – those RMs reported no canola that year, and Chapter 19 has to decide how to colour them. Mapping this object is where that chapter starts.

title: 18  Working with Spatial Data in R
text:
18.5 Which polygon holds a point
A spatial join matches rows by location instead of by key. st_join() attaches to each point the attributes of the polygon it falls in:


# Which RM is each city in?
st_join(cities_sf, rms) |>
  select(city, RMNO, RMNM)

> # Which RM is each city in?
> st_join(cities_sf, rms) |>
+   select(city, RMNO, RMNM)

Geometry type: POINT
Dimension:     XY

Geodetic CRS:  WGS 84
# A tibble: 4 × 4
  city          RMNO  RMNM                 geometry
  <chr>         <chr> <chr>             <POINT [°]>
1 Saskatoon     344   CORMAN PARK   (-106.67 52.13)
2 Regina        159   SHERWOOD      (-104.61 50.45)
3 Swift Current 137   SWIFT CURRENT (-107.79 50.28)
4 Yorkton       244   ORKNEY        (-102.46 51.21)



Counting many points per polygon is the same join followed by count(). Module 8 uses exactly that to summarize thousands of machinery points inside a field boundary (Chapter 24).

title: 18  Working with Spatial Data in R
text:
18.6 Reading raster data
The terra package does for rasters what sf does for vectors. rast() reads the file, and printing the object answers the Chapter 17 questions – how many cells, how big each one is, how much ground they cover, and in what CRS:


# Load the package for raster data
library(terra)

# Read the crop inventory slice
aci <- rast("data/aci_rm_slice_2023.tif")

# Size, resolution, extent and CRS in one printout
aci

> # Load the package for raster data
> library(terra)
> 
> # Read the crop inventory slice
> aci <- rast("data/aci_rm_slice_2023.tif")
> 
> # Size, resolution, extent and CRS in one printout
> aci
class       : SpatRaster
size        : 1029, 2136, 1  (nrow, ncol, nlyr)
resolution  : 30, 30  (x, y)
extent      : 409980, 474060, 5689170, 5720040  (xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax)
coord. ref. : WGS 84 / UTM zone 13N (EPSG:32613)
source      : aci_rm_slice_2023.tif
name        : aci_rm_slice_2023



The slice covers the RMs of Wood Creek and McCraney at 30 metres, and its CRS is already UTM Zone 13. Figure 18.2 puts the boundaries over the cells.

# Shrink for display: each 8-by-8 block of cells becomes one cell
aci_small <- aggregate(aci, fact = 8, fun = "modal")

# The class table pairs each value with a crop name and a colour
classes <- read_csv("data/aci_crop_classes.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

# Raster to a data frame of cell centres and values
aci_df <- as.data.frame(aci_small, xy = TRUE) |>
  rename(value = 3) |>                     # the third column holds the class
  left_join(classes, by = "value")         # attach names and colours

# The named palette for the classes present
pal <- aci_df |>
  distinct(crop, colour) |>
  deframe()

# The two RM boundaries, in the raster's CRS
pair <- rms_utm |>
  filter(RMNO %in% c("281", "282"))

ggplot() +
  geom_raster(data = aci_df, aes(x, y, fill = crop)) +
  geom_sf(data = pair, fill = NA, colour = "black", linewidth = 0.5) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = pal) +
  theme_void() +
  # A compact legend leaves more room for the map
  theme(legend.key.size = unit(4, "mm"),
        legend.text = element_text(size = 8)) +
  labs(fill = NULL)







Figure 18.2: The 2023 Annual Crop Inventory over the RMs of Wood Creek (281, right) and McCraney (282, left), with the RM boundaries as a vector layer on top.





The overlay works because both layers are in the same CRS. Had the boundaries stayed in degrees, the outlines would land nowhere near the cells – the rule from Chapter 17, in raster form.
